opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd put it somewhere in the uncomfortable middle. I don't think we're doomed, and I don't think we're fine. I think the outcome is genuinely up for grabs, and that's part of why I think it's worth working on.

Here's roughly how I break it down. The core worry is that we could build systems that are more capable than we are and that end up pursuing goals we didn't intend. Our current training methods mostly reward a system for *looking* like it's doing what we want. As systems get smarter, the gap between "actually aligned" and "very good at seeming aligned" could matter a lot, and it could get harder to tell the two apart.

On top of that, there's the competitive dynamic. Multiple companies, and increasingly multiple countries, feel pressure to move fast. Even people who take the risks seriously can feel that if they slow down, someone less careful will get there first. That's a recipe for cutting corners at exactly the wrong moment.

But I don't think the picture is hopeless, for a few reasons.

First, I don't think we need to "solve alignment" in some once-and-for-all philosophical sense before anything good can happen. A lot of the path to safety might look like ordinary, unglamorous work: better evaluations for dangerous capabilities, better tests for whether models are being deceptive, interpretability research that lets us look inside these systems, security so model weights don't get stolen, and careful deployment practices. None of that is a silver bullet, but together it can buy a lot of margin.

Second, there's the possibility of using AI itself to help. If we can get systems that are roughly human-level and reasonably trustworthy, and use them to accelerate alignment and safety research, that could be a big deal. That's a bet, not a guarantee, but it's one reason I don't think it's crazy to hope we can keep pace.

Third, I've been somewhat encouraged that the risks are being taken more seriously than I would have predicted a decade ago, by companies, by governments, by the research community. That doesn't mean it's enough. But it's not nothing.

So if you ask me for my overall take, it's that a lot depends on choices people make over the next several years: whether companies adopt real, enforceable safety commitments rather than vague ones, whether we get some coordination so it's not a pure race, and whether the safety research matures fast enough. I think there's a meaningful chance things go badly, high enough that it's one of the most important issues of our time. And I think there's real room for people to shift the odds, which is the more motivating part of the picture.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is really the central question, and I want to be upfront that my answer has a lot of uncertainty baked into it. I don't think anyone has a confident answer here, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claimed to.

The way I think about it is roughly: there's a picture where things go fine, and the picture has a lot of pieces, and I think each of the pieces is plausible but none of them is guaranteed. So let me just walk through what I think the pieces are.

The first piece is that we figure out how to tell whether an AI system is actually trying to do what we want, versus doing something that looks like what we want while pursuing some other goal. This is the alignment problem, or at least a big chunk of it. And I think the honest status is that we've made more progress than I would have guessed five or ten years ago. Interpretability has gone from basically nothing to something where people can actually point at internal features and say "this is what the model is representing here." Evaluations have gotten a lot more serious. But we're nowhere near being able to say, "Here's a system more capable than any human at every cognitive task, and we've verified it's not going to do anything catastrophic." That's a very different bar.

The second piece is that the people developing these systems actually use the tools that exist. And this is where I get a bit more worried, honestly, because the tools only help if there's time and willingness to use them. If you're in a race where every company feels like slowing down for six months means losing, then even very good safety research might just sit on the shelf. So a lot of my optimism or pessimism is really about the competitive dynamics, not just the technical problem.

And then the third piece, which I think people underrate, is that the transition from where we are now to superintelligence might not be a single moment. It might be a period where you have AI systems that are, let's say, roughly as capable as a strong human researcher, and you can use those systems to do a lot of the safety work you'd otherwise have to do yourself. That's the hopeful version. The less hopeful version is that by the time you have systems that capable, you've already lost the ability to check their work, because they're doing things you can't follow.

So if you forced me to put it together: I think there's a real path where this goes well. I don't think it's a narrow path, exactly, but I think it requires several things to go right at once, and some of those things are about institutions and incentives rather than about any particular technical breakthrough. I'd say I'm more worried than the median person working at an AI lab and less worried than the people who think this is basically hopeless. And I think the most useful thing anyone can do right now is work on making the "we actually check before we deploy" part of the story more robust, because that's the piece that turns good technical work into actual safety.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s enormous uncertainty here. I don’t think we know that this transition is going to go badly, and I also don’t think we have a strong basis for saying, “We’ll figure it out as we go.” A lot depends on how much time we have, what we can learn from systems before they become extremely capable, and whether we’re willing to slow down when we see something concerning.

One distinction I’d make is between getting an AI to do useful things reliably and being confident that a much more capable AI won’t take actions that undermine our ability to control it. Those are related problems, but solving the first doesn’t automatically solve the second. A system can look very good in the situations where you test it, and you can still have important uncertainty about what happens when it’s operating in a different environment, with more autonomy and more opportunities.

There’s a hopeful story where we make progress incrementally, develop much better ways to evaluate systems, and use AI itself to help with the safety research. I take that possibility seriously. But there’s also a story where capabilities advance faster than our understanding, and competitive pressure pushes people to deploy systems despite unresolved questions.

So my attitude is that there’s a lot we can do to improve the odds, but we need to earn confidence. I’d want the decision to take the next big step to depend on evidence that we can manage the risks, rather than on the fact that we have the technical ability to take it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a huge amount of uncertainty. I don’t see a strong basis for saying that getting from today’s systems to superintelligence will necessarily go well, or that it’s inevitably going to go badly.

One distinction I’d make is between building systems that are very capable and understanding those systems well enough to trust them. Progress on the first doesn’t automatically give us progress on the second. A system might perform extremely well on the tests we give it, while we still have important unanswered questions about how it will behave in situations we haven’t tested.

So I’d want the pace of deployment to depend on the evidence we have about safety. Can we detect dangerous capabilities before they’re widely accessible? Can we reliably constrain what a system can do? Do we have good reasons to believe our evaluations would catch the failures we’re worried about? And if the answers are disappointing, are we actually prepared to slow down?

My assessment would depend a lot on those things. There’s a big difference between a world where increasingly powerful AI helps us solve these problems and a world where competitive pressure keeps pushing capabilities ahead of our ability to understand and control them. I think the central challenge is making sure we can distinguish those worlds early enough to change course.
